An app card adds an app's information or actions to a HubSpot record. It can put a related invoice status beside a deal or help a user start a process while reviewing that record.

I would start with the decision someone needs to make. If a small piece of context helps them make it, a card may be enough. The data source, permissions and maintenance still need an owner.

App cards and native record cards are different

HubSpot provides native record cards for properties, associations and other record information. Some can be configured in the record editor without building an app. HubSpot documents these options in Use cards on records.

An app card is supplied by an app. Modern app cards use React-based UI extensions and can display CRM or external data and support actions. Supported surfaces include record pages, preview panels and help desk sidebars, depending on the card's configuration. See the UI extensions overview.

A card in the right sidebar could use either modern or legacy technology. Its position alone does not identify the implementation.

Check existing options before building

Begin with the information already in HubSpot. A native property or association card may answer the question once the layout is configured.

Next, check your installed apps and suitable Marketplace apps. Confirm that the vendor supplies the card you need, which objects and locations it supports, and what account access or subscription it requires. Installation alone does not establish that the right users have the right card in their record view.

Custom development fits when a specific decision needs data or behavior those options do not provide. Agree who will maintain the app, its connected services and the record layout.

Scope one useful task

Possible tasks include checking an invoice status, showing a business-specific calculation or starting a delivery process in another system. Each needs its own data mapping and implementation; they are examples to scope rather than features every card includes.

My renewal-status card shows a focused example. It reads the linked license information and presents a status on the deal. It is read-only, with the lookup and hosting boundaries described in the case.

For a card that changes another system, define the allowed action, who can perform it and how success or failure is shown. I would make the read-only view useful before adding a write action.

Agree how the data and access work

A card's usefulness depends on correct record matching and a maintained source. Decide whether it reads stored CRM values, requests current information or uses a cached result. Show when information is unavailable or too old for the decision.

External data access needs a configured connection and backend. HubSpot's data-fetching guide covers permitted URLs and request handling. Apps using Sensitive Data scopes cannot use hubspot.fetch(); have the developer check the restrictions before promising an external lookup.

Test the intended users, permissions and record types. Include missing associations, source outages and repeated clicks on any action. Document credentials, hosting, monitoring and who handles a broken connection. A card displaying live information is still dependent on the systems behind it.

Check legacy cards separately

HubSpot's older announcement gives 31 October 2026 for the classic CRM card sunset. The current migration guide says removal from customer views is 2 November, with migration tooling available until 1 December. The tooling window does not extend the cards' visibility through November.

I would plan to finish before 31 October and confirm the current guidance with the app owner. The classic CRM card migration guide explains the source conflict, replacement testing and view migration. This retirement concerns the legacy technology, not every record card.

Decide whether the work is worth maintaining

Compare the repeated lookup or missed step with the effort of building and maintaining the card. Check whether users act on the information and whether a simpler record layout solves the problem.

The custom app cards page describes the development scope and platform conditions. Questions about a particular record interface? You're welcome to compare notes.

AEO means Answer Engine Optimization: improving how a business is represented in AI-generated answers. For a small team, I would begin with the questions buyers ask and the information they need to judge your work.

HubSpot AEO can help monitor that visibility. Whether it is worth using depends on what you will do with the findings and how you will assess the result.

What HubSpot AEO measures

HubSpot's current AEO setup guide describes tracking prompts across ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. It reports brand visibility, competitors and citations, with recommendations for improvement. Data collection begins after setup, and tracked prompts run daily.

These results describe the prompts and engines being tracked. A brand mention, a citation linking to your site and a visit to that site are different observations. Review them separately before connecting them to leads or revenue.

Content work still needs someone to choose the changes, check the facts and maintain the pages. A monitoring dashboard gives that person evidence to investigate.

What the search research can tell you

Pew Research Center's July 2025 analysis used browsing data from 900 U.S. adults during March 2025. Visits to Google results with an AI summary led to a traditional-result click 8% of the time, compared with 15% without a summary. Clicks on a link inside the summary occurred on 1% of visits to pages with a summary.

That is a useful observation about that sample and period. It does not measure your site's traffic loss, establish that the summary caused the difference or describe all ChatGPT searches. I would use it as a reason to inspect your own acquisition channels, rather than a forecast for your business.

Check access, cost and the work involved

As checked on 22 October 2026, HubSpot advertises standalone HubSpot AEO at $50 USD per month, before applicable tax. AEO is also included in Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise. Features, permissions and usage limits differ between the standalone and Marketing Hub experiences; check the current packaging for your account.

The subscription is only part of the cost. Someone needs time to select prompts, inspect citations and improve content. If you already have access, I would still define that work before enabling a pilot.

HubSpot's free AEO Grader provides a one-time diagnostic. The paid AEO product supports ongoing tracking. Choose the level of measurement that answers your question.

Make the existing information useful first

Start with clear pages about your expertise, the problems you work on and evidence for your claims. Answer practical buyer questions, keep product details current and make important information available as readable text. Explain what a case demonstrates and where its limits are.

For Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, Google says existing SEO fundamentals still apply. It does not require special AI markup or a new machine-readable file. A page must be indexed and eligible for a search snippet to qualify as a supporting link; meeting the requirements does not guarantee inclusion.

I would fix inaccessible pages, unclear service descriptions and unsupported claims before producing more articles. Use a clear contact route and make sure enquiries reach someone who can respond. The onboarding checks cover ownership and handovers inside HubSpot.

Run a pilot around real buyer questions

Choose a small set of questions from sales conversations, support requests or the decisions your audience needs to make. Include unbranded questions and relevant comparisons. Check that the prompts use your buyers' language and location.

Record a baseline, keep the prompt set stable and inspect the answers and cited pages. HubSpot recommends reviewing prompt performance over multiple days or weeks because responses change. Note content changes and other campaigns so a change in visibility is not automatically credited to one edit.

Alongside mentions and citations, review identifiable referral visits, useful enquiries and what those visitors do next. Some discovery will not produce a trackable click. Record that measurement limit rather than treating every mention as a lead.

Decide what the findings help you change

I would continue when the tracking reveals relevant gaps and the team can act on them. If the main findings are already-known content problems, address those before expanding the tool or publishing schedule.

The Breeze guide takes the same task-first approach to HubSpot's other AI features. Questions about your own evaluation? You're welcome to compare notes.

If marketing calls every form submission an MQL while sales expects a qualified buyer, a workflow will pass that disagreement straight into the CRM. I would start with a written definition that both teams can use.

Then check which changes HubSpot already makes. Add automation for the decisions your process still needs, with someone responsible for reviewing exceptions.

Lifecycle stage, deal stage and lead status

Lifecycle stage describes a contact or company's relationship with your business. Deal stage describes a specific sales opportunity; one contact can have several deals. Lead status describes sales follow-up, such as Attempted to Contact or Connected. HubSpot positions it within the SQL lifecycle stage. See HubSpot's property definitions.

HubSpot includes eight default lifecycle stages, which you can customize. Use them as a starting point for your own definitions:

Stage	Practical meaning
Subscriber	Signed up to hear from you.
Lead	Interacted beyond a subscription, such as submitting an enquiry.
Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL)	Marketing considers the record ready for sales.
Sales Qualified Lead (SQL)	Sales considers the record a potential customer.
Opportunity	Associated with a deal.
Customer	Has become a customer; define the purchase event that sets this.
Evangelist	A customer who advocates for the business.
Other	Does not fit the other categories.

HubSpot's lifecycle guide documents the defaults and update behavior. Keep activities such as attempted calls in lead status, so the lifecycle property can describe the broader relationship.

Agree what qualifies an MQL and SQL

For MQL, separate fit from engagement. Fit might mean a relevant role, company size or market. Engagement might mean a demo request or a scoring threshold. A pricing-page visit alone says little about whether the person is a plausible buyer.

Write a rule the team can check: “A contact becomes an MQL when they meet our fit criteria and show the agreed engagement.” Specify the actual properties and thresholds before building.

For SQL, agree what sales must review and accept. Assigning a contact to a rep is not evidence that the review happened. A sales-acceptance checkpoint can use a custom review property, with an owner and a rejection reason. It does not have to become another lifecycle stage.

For rejected or poorly timed leads, keep the review outcome separate from lifecycle stage when you need to retain qualification history. Decide how those records can be reconsidered later.

Check native automation before adding workflows

Under Settings → Objects → Contacts → Lifecycle Stage → Automate, review the settings already enabled:

Record creation: a default stage can be set for new contacts and companies. Check form-level defaults and connected-app behavior too.
Deals: creation of the first associated deal, or a deal being won, can set a selected lifecycle stage on associated contacts and companies.
Associated leads: a setting can update lifecycle stage when a lead is associated. Leads created by automation are an exception.
Company sync: the primary company's stage can update associated contacts. A contact's stage does not update its company through this setting.

These settings move stages forward. Check the automation rules and exceptions before enabling them, including what happens to existing records. A missing association needs investigation; another workflow cannot identify the right customer by itself.

Add workflows for your qualification rules

Use the native deal settings where they fit. For custom qualification, a possible design is:

Lead to MQL: enroll contacts at the intended starting stage who meet the agreed fit and engagement filters. Set MQL, then notify the owner or create a task if needed.
MQL to SQL: use an explicit acceptance decision, such as a custom MQL Review property set to Accepted. Record rejection reasons separately and define the follow-up responsibility.
Review stalled records: flag contacts that have stayed in MQL or SQL without relevant activity. A quarterly review of records older than 90 days is an example; choose a threshold that fits your sales cycle.

The workflow property-update action requires a Professional or Enterprise account. Confirm the actions available in your subscription before choosing the design.

Test a small set of records first: an eligible lead, an existing customer, a rejected MQL and a record with missing associations. Check enrollment and re-enrollment rules, property history and any notifications. Existing customers should not be treated as new MQLs because they submit another form.

For stage-based review, use the entry date or the time since lifecycle stage changed. HubSpot's calculated latest/cumulative time values have special behavior while a record is still in a stage; check the property guidance before using them as triggers.

Correct existing records in controlled batches

Start with evidence you trust, such as purchase records, deal history and recorded qualification decisions. Keep uncertain cases for review rather than forcing every record into a guessed stage.

Before a bulk import or workflow update:

Export record IDs and current values, and identify automation that could react to the change.
Agree the mapping and review a representative sample with marketing and sales.
Test a small batch, inspect property history and downstream effects, then expand the update.
Assign an owner to unresolved records and repeat the check after the next relevant data refresh.

You can manually move a stage backward. Imports, forms, APIs and workflows require the current value to be cleared before setting an earlier stage. A manual backward move can reset legacy “Became a” dates; newer calculated history properties behave differently. Check the documented date effects before clearing or resetting values. A property export alone does not restore every historical date or downstream action.

Measure the handover using your own definitions

For MQL-to-SQL conversion, define the MQL cohort and how long it has to reach SQL. Measure the proportion accepted under the same criteria, then compare sources and rejection reasons. A generic benchmark cannot tell you whether the issue is fit, follow-up or a different definition of SQL.

My data quality case shows how I separate a detected mismatch from the decision to correct it. For the surrounding sales process, see my pipeline review approach.

Questions about the setup? You're welcome to compare notes.

Stage	Practical meaning

Lead	Interacted beyond a subscription, such as submitting an enquiry.
Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL)	Marketing considers the record ready for sales.
Sales Qualified Lead (SQL)	Sales considers the record a potential customer.
Opportunity	Associated with a deal.
Customer	Has become a customer; define the purchase event that sets this.
Evangelist	A customer who advocates for the business.
Other	Does not fit the other categories.

HubSpot's lifecycle guide documents the defaults and update behavior. Keep activities such as attempted calls in lead status, so the lifecycle property can describe the broader relationship.

For MQL, separate fit from engagement. Fit might mean a relevant role, company size or market. Engagement might mean a demo request or a scoring threshold. A pricing-page visit alone says little about whether the person is a plausible buyer.

Write a rule the team can check: “A contact becomes an MQL when they meet our fit criteria and show the agreed engagement.” Specify the actual properties and thresholds before building.

For SQL, agree what sales must review and accept. Assigning a contact to a rep is not evidence that the review happened. A sales-acceptance checkpoint can use a custom review property, with an owner and a rejection reason. It does not have to become another lifecycle stage.

For rejected or poorly timed leads, keep the review outcome separate from lifecycle stage when you need to retain qualification history. Decide how those records can be reconsidered later.

Record creation: a default stage can be set for new contacts and companies. Check form-level defaults and connected-app behavior too.
Deals: creation of the first associated deal, or a deal being won, can set a selected lifecycle stage on associated contacts and companies.

Lead to MQL: enroll contacts at the intended starting stage who meet the agreed fit and engagement filters. Set MQL, then notify the owner or create a task if needed.

Review stalled records: flag contacts that have stayed in MQL or SQL without relevant activity. A quarterly review of records older than 90 days is an example; choose a threshold that fits your sales cycle.

Correct existing records in controlled batches

Start with evidence you trust, such as purchase records, deal history and recorded qualification decisions. Keep uncertain cases for review rather than forcing every record into a guessed stage.

Before a bulk import or workflow update:

Export record IDs and current values, and identify automation that could react to the change.
Agree the mapping and review a representative sample with marketing and sales.
Test a small batch, inspect property history and downstream effects, then expand the update.

A property export alone does not restore every historical date or downstream action.

HubSpot is retiring classic, also called legacy, CRM cards. If an installed app or custom integration uses one, identify its owner and confirm the replacement. The position of a card in the sidebar alone does not tell you which technology it uses.

I would keep this work focused: preserve the information and actions people need, test the replacement, then remove the old card when migration is complete.

Check the dates against the current migration guide

HubSpot's official pages currently differ. As checked on 21 October 2026:

Source	What it says
Changelog	The sunset is 31 October 2026. New Marketplace apps containing classic cards have not been accepted since 16 June 2025.
Migration guide	Legacy cards are removed from customer views on 2 November 2026. The migration UI and API remain available until 1 December 2026, then are discontinued.

My planning recommendation is to finish before 31 October. The tooling window is not a promise that cards remain visible through November. Confirm the current guidance with the app owner before scheduling production changes.

Identify which cards are affected

This sunset concerns cards built with the legacy CRM extensions technology. It does not mean that every HubSpot record card or every installed app is being retired. React-based app cards are the replacement.

List the apps and custom integrations that add information to CRM records. For each candidate, record:

The card, record types and locations where people use it.
The vendor or internal developer responsible for it.
Whether it uses legacy technology, and the replacement or removal plan.

Ask the owner to confirm the implementation and migration status. Avoid assuming that a large vendor has already migrated, or that an undocumented custom card is safe because it still loads. Ask about the effect on the wider integration too; the card sunset does not guarantee that every other app feature is unaffected.

Choose what to replace, rebuild or remove

For a vendor app, ask for its rollout plan and how to verify the updated card in your account. For custom work, decide whether to reproduce the existing behavior, redesign the card or remove it if it no longer serves a task.

UI extensions use React and can show CRM or external data and support actions. The useful scope depends on data access, permissions and the system behind the card. A migration does not need to become a broader interface project.

My read-only renewal-status card is one example of a focused record interface. The app cards guide explains the wider options.

Build and test the replacement

HubSpot provides a Legacy CRM Card Converter example. Check its documented differences and adapt it to your existing card’s data and actions.

Have the developer follow the current migration guide for the app type and project version. Test in a separate environment before replacing cards in customer views. Include:

Normal records and missing or unavailable associated data.
Written status labels, permissions and any actions the card supports.
Each relevant record type and workspace location.

Ticket cards need particular attention: the migration guide describes separate replacements for the CRM sidebar and help desk sidebar. Confirm both if the legacy card appears in both places.

Replace views only after verification

Building a replacement card and replacing existing user views are separate steps. HubSpot supports view migration through the projects UI or migrate views API. For migrated Marketplace apps, release flags can affect replacement-card visibility and must be handled before the view migration.

View migration cannot be reversed once started. Confirm the replacement and its visibility first, then follow the migration procedure. Verify the completed views, document the new owner and remove the legacy card when it is safe to do so.

The amount of work depends on the card's behavior and dependencies. Estimate it after the inventory and replacement test.

Questions about a particular card? You're welcome to get in touch.

I would start with a task the team repeats and can judge: preparing for a call, answering a common support question or reviewing an outreach draft. That gives you something concrete to test before expanding your use of AI.

Breeze covers an evolving set of assistants, agents and AI features in HubSpot. This guide focuses on everyday assistance, support, content, prospecting and data enrichment. Check each feature's requirements separately; sharing a brand name does not mean sharing access or billing rules.

Breeze Assistant: start with a task you can check

HubSpot's current documentation calls the conversational tool Breeze Assistant. Older material may refer to Breeze Copilot. The assistant can summarize records, prepare for meetings and help generate content. Its actions depend on user permissions, AI settings and connected tools. Check the Assistant requirements.

For a small pilot, ask for a summary of a familiar account or a draft follow-up based on a known conversation. Compare the response with the underlying records. Check dates, missing activity and any claims the draft makes before using it.

I would judge whether it reduces the work of finding and checking information. A fluent summary is useful only if it reflects the right customer context.

Customer Agent: check the sources and human handover

Customer Agent can use knowledge base content, website pages, imported URLs and uploaded files. It is not restricted to a HubSpot knowledge base. HubSpot explains how to manage its knowledge sources.

Start with a defined category of questions and maintained answers. Include questions the agent should hand to a person, then test whether that handover reaches the right team. Track incorrect answers and repeat contacts alongside the number of conversations handled.

Source selection matters: HubSpot notes that private source content can still appear in customer-facing responses even when the source itself is not cited. Review what is appropriate to expose before adding it. Give someone responsibility for updating the answers as policies change.

Content Agent: use the context, then edit the draft

Content Agent can draw on account context and brand voice settings to produce content. The current documented beta lists Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise as a requirement for its features across tools. Review its requirements and supported content types, rather than assuming every content feature is included with Content Hub.

I would try it on an outline or a variation of content you already know. Check the facts, positioning and promises, then read it against your own writing style. Brand voice settings help provide direction; they do not replace editorial judgement.

Measure the work through approval, including corrections and rewriting. The time taken to generate a draft is only part of the task.

Prospecting Agent: review the audience and the message

Prospecting Agent supports prospect research and outreach through configured plays. Its email review settings distinguish reviewing messages before sending from sending without review.

I would begin with review enabled and a narrow audience. Confirm the fit criteria, existing customer relationships and contact ownership before enrolling records. Read the research and messages against what sales actually knows about those accounts.

Then measure accepted recommendations, relevant replies and corrections needed. An activation count or a high volume of generated emails does not tell you whether the targeting works. Agree who handles replies and removes unsuitable contacts from the process.

Data enrichment: check eligibility and overwrite behavior

Treat the older Breeze Intelligence label as a starting point for finding the current enrichment documentation. HubSpot now states that data enrichment does not consume HubSpot Credits, while smart properties do. The enrichment overview explains that distinction and the subscription requirements.

Coverage still depends on the record. Contacts need a business email and companies need a domain; available information varies. Automatic, manual and continuous enrichment also differ in how they fill or replace values. Check enrichment behavior before using it on existing records.

I would test a relevant sample and review the fields that matter to your process. Decide which source owns each value, especially where another system also writes to HubSpot. A headcount or database-size threshold alone is a poor reason to enable or reject enrichment.

Check access and usage costs before the pilot

HubSpot Credits apply to specific usage-based features. Availability also depends on subscription and seats. Check the current consumption rules, included allowance and overage settings in your account; a quoted dollar price from an older announcement is not a complete cost estimate. HubSpot's credit guide links to the current product catalog.

Before testing, write down what counts as a useful result and how you will stop or limit the pilot. Include the cost of review and maintaining source content. For support, also distinguish a resolved conversation from one that returns later or needs a person.

Keep the data and review process in scope

Choose a task with a clear owner, usable source information and an observable result. Keep the pilot small enough to inspect the outputs and investigate exceptions before increasing its reach.

My data quality case shows how I separate a detected mismatch from the decision to correct a record. The lifecycle stage guide covers the qualification definitions that prospecting and handovers depend on.

Questions about a particular setup? You're welcome to compare notes.

I would start with the work you need done and the person responsible for delivering it. A contractor or agency label tells you little about whether that person understands your CRM model, migration or integration.

For focused HubSpot work, direct access to a specialist can be a good fit. A project with several simultaneous workstreams may need a delivery team. Establish which situation you have before comparing proposals.

When a contractor can fit

Consider a contractor when the scope is focused and the work can be sequenced: reviewing a pipeline, building an integration or improving a defined part of the CRM. Ask whether the person proposing the work will also design, build and document it.

Direct access can make decisions easier to follow. It still needs agreed scope, a change process and time from your own team. Confirm availability, other commitments and what happens during absence. If the work needs another specialism, establish who brings it in and who remains accountable.

When an agency can fit

Consider an agency when you need several disciplines working at the same time, coordinated delivery across teams or continuing capacity beyond one person's availability. A multi-hub migration alongside content and integration work may require that structure.

Ask for the actual project team and its allocated capacity. An agency name alone does not establish who is available or how specialist work is reviewed. Confirm who makes decisions, how context passes between people and how team changes are handled.

Your procurement process may also affect the choice. Check its supplier requirements early with your own procurement team, then compare providers that can meet them.

Compare total scope and cost

Ask both providers to price the same deliverables and assumptions. A useful proposal separates discovery, configuration, data work, testing, training and post-launch support. It should explain what is included, what depends on your team and how changes are priced.

For hourly work, compare the estimated effort and the people doing it. For a fixed fee, check the acceptance criteria and excluded work. For a retainer, confirm the capacity or outputs included and how priorities are agreed.

Include software subscriptions, connector costs and ongoing maintenance where relevant. A lower hourly rate does not establish a lower total cost, and a larger team does not guarantee an earlier finish. Ask each provider to explain the schedule's dependencies and review points.

Published rate examples can describe a particular supplier or market. They do not establish universal contractor and agency prices. Use comparable proposals for your own scope instead of a promised percentage saving.

Ask for relevant evidence and a delivery plan

These questions help evaluate either model:

Who will do the work? Name the responsible specialist and the people reviewing it. Agree how staffing changes will be communicated.
What similar problem have they solved? Ask what they built, which decisions they owned and what remained open. A related integration or data model is more useful evidence than a logo alone.
What do they need from your team? Plan stakeholder decisions, data access, process definitions and review time. Someone internally must own the business rules.
How will changes be tested? Ask about sample records, migration checks, approval before live updates and handling exceptions.
What happens after launch? Confirm documentation, administrator access, training, maintenance ownership and the boundary of ongoing support.

My Account-based CRM case is an example of describing design, implementation and recurring review separately. My consultancy approach also distinguishes review recommendations from implementation scope.

Treat partner status and AI as context

HubSpot partner tiers involve sourced, assisted and managed points linked to recurring revenue, with additional program requirements. They are not simply a count of completed implementations. HubSpot documents how tier points work.

I would still ask about the assigned person's relevant experience and the team's review process. Partner status is one piece of information about the organization.

The same applies to AI tooling. Ask which tasks use AI and who checks the output before it changes CRM data or reaches customers. A claim about faster drafting does not establish that one person can cover every role in a project.

Choose around the work and continuity you need

For a contained problem, a specialist with clear ownership may be enough. Where work needs to run in parallel, evaluate the team's coordination and capacity. In both cases, agree the scope and handover before starting.

I would start a HubSpot rollout by agreeing what the team needs to do in it. That means defining the process, preparing the records and naming the people responsible for decisions.

The checks below cover both a new setup and an existing account that needs attention. They give you a way to review the work before expanding it.

1. Building before agreeing the process

Map how a lead arrives, becomes qualified and passes to sales. Define who owns each handover and what evidence allows a deal to move forward. Include rejected leads and purchases completed outside HubSpot.

Use real examples to resolve disagreements before configuring stages. A short process document gives the team something concrete to test against.

2. Assuming onboarding includes every implementation task

HubSpot describes its onboarding as technical and strategic guidance tailored to your goals, products and technology stack. The delivery scope still needs to be explicit.

Check who configures the account, cleans and migrates data, builds integrations, tests changes and trains users. Record what your own team must deliver. Avoid estimating the schedule from the word “onboarding” alone; the work and dependencies determine it.

3. Importing without a record-matching plan

Review duplicates, field formats and missing values before importing. Decide how records will be identified and associated. HubSpot supports Record ID for existing records, with Email and Company domain name among the other identifiers available for contacts and companies. Follow the import requirements for your objects.

I would test a small sample, then check updates, new records and associations before importing the rest. Preserve relevant subscription and suppression information during migration; excluding someone from a campaign does not automatically mean deleting their CRM history.

4. Leaving lifecycle and deal stages undefined

Lifecycle stages describe a contact or company's relationship with the business. Deal stages describe progress through a sales process. Agree what qualification, sales acceptance and becoming a customer mean in your setup.

If purchases happen elsewhere, decide how that evidence reaches HubSpot. The lifecycle stage guide covers the native settings, automation options and care needed when correcting existing records.

5. Automating rules the team has not tested

Begin with a process people can explain and records they trust. Add automation where its inputs, expected result and owner are clear.

Test normal records, missing information and records that should be excluded. Check repeat enrollment and what happens when another system updates the same field. Keep workflows focused enough to investigate, and agree how to stop one if it behaves unexpectedly. Automation can support adoption; its rollout needs the same review as the rest of the setup.

6. Treating training as the end of adoption

Name an internal owner for questions and changes. Give that person time to maintain the setup, with a sponsor who can resolve disagreements about business rules.

Train people on their actual tasks and reports. After launch, review incomplete handovers, missing activity and work still happening elsewhere. Use those findings to adjust the process and training. Include CRM training in the plan for new colleagues.

7. Creating properties without a clear use

Check the meaning of an existing property before adding another. For a new property, record its purpose, owner, allowed values and where the value comes from. Decide who needs to see or edit it.

Review forms and record layouts around the task the user is doing. Remove unused fields only after checking their dependencies in workflows, reports and integrations. A field that looks empty may still be part of an active process.

8. Connecting systems without ownership rules

For each integration, document which system owns each field, the sync direction and what happens when values disagree. Check associations and record matching alongside property updates.

Test conflicting updates and sync failures before enabling the connection broadly. My data quality case shows how I separate a detected mismatch from the decision to correct a record. Finding a difference is the start of the review.

9. Overlooking marketing contact settings and billing

First check whether your subscription uses marketing contacts. In that model, marketing contacts count towards the paid contact tier; non-marketing contacts do not. Marketing status is a billing designation, separate from email subscription preferences. HubSpot explains which tools use marketing contacts.

Review the settings for imports, forms and connected tools before adding records. Monitor the current count, tier limit and next update date. Under the documented marketing-contact model, exceeding the tier triggers an upgrade. Changing contacts to non-marketing takes effect on the next update date. Purchased tiers can only be downgraded at renewal under these rules. Check the billing rules for your account, including the maximum marketing contacts setting.

I would resolve this before a large import. Keep subscription preferences intact and agree who can change marketing status.

Agree what is ready for launch

Choose a first process the team can complete from start to finish. Confirm the records, ownership and reports support it, then give users a route to report problems. Keep unfinished work in an owned list with clear priorities.

If you are reviewing an existing setup, start with a sample of recent leads or deals and follow their handovers. Questions about what you find? You're welcome to compare notes.

HubSpot's spring announcements raised useful questions about agent costs, data preparation and custom apps. I would evaluate them against a task your team already needs to complete.

This article was first published in April and reviewed on 22 October 2026. The sections below distinguish the spring announcements from current documentation. The August developer deadline has passed; the classic CRM card migration still needs attention.

Breeze pricing: distinguish the announcement from your account cost

In April, HubSpot announced outcome-based pricing for Customer Agent and Prospecting Agent, paid through HubSpot Credits. The announcement tied charges to resolved conversations and leads recommended for outreach.

That billing event does not establish the quality of every answer or recommendation. I would include corrections, repeat contacts and human review when evaluating the result.

For a new pilot, check current access, credit rates, included allowance and overage settings in your account. HubSpot's credit guide explains the usage model. The Breeze guide covers practical checks for the individual use cases.

Agents in workflows: define what happens after the output

The current Run Agent documentation describes choosing an agent already added to the account, providing inputs and using its output in later workflow actions. It requires an eligible Professional or Enterprise subscription and HubSpot Credits. Do not assume every Breeze product can be invoked through this action.

Start with narrow enrollment criteria and review the result before allowing it to update important fields or trigger customer communication. Test missing data, repeat enrollment and failure handling. Assign someone to investigate unexpected output and check the current execution limits before expanding.

Data Hub: focus on the dataset you need

Data Hub replaced Operations Hub in September 2025. Its launch predates Spring 2026.

Data Studio combines data from HubSpot and external sources in a spreadsheet-style interface. It is available with Data Hub Professional and Enterprise; activating data outside the studio can consume credits.

I would begin with one question your current reports cannot answer reliably. Define the join keys, source refresh and calculation, then compare the dataset with a known sample. Check supported connectors and activation costs for that use case. A visual interface still needs clear rules for what each row and value means.

Quoting: test the answers and the human handover

Closing Agent can answer buyer questions on a quote using the knowledge supplied to it. The current setup guide labels it beta and lists Revenue Hub Professional or Enterprise, with seat requirements. Older material refers to Commerce Hub.

Test questions about scope, pricing and terms against approved information. Include questions that need the quote owner or another team, then verify the configured handover. For any AI-drafted quote content, review the line items, totals and promises before sending it to a buyer.

I would evaluate this on a controlled set of quotes before making it part of the normal sales process.

Custom apps: keep the interface as small as the task

The spring developer release expanded App Homes into multi-page App Pages and described sharing code across UI extensions with npm workspaces. A full app page can suit a task that spans records; a focused app card may be enough for information needed on one record.

Platform 2026.03 also restored HubSpot-hosted serverless functions. Hosted app functions require Enterprise access or a developer test account; public endpoints require Content Hub Enterprise and are not available in developer test accounts. Check the current migration path and limits for your app before choosing its hosting approach.

My renewal-status card is an example of keeping a record interface focused on one decision.

Developer dates: August has passed, and card guidance differs

The spring developer release set 1 August 2026 as the end of support for Projects 2025.1, with builds on that version failing. That date is now in the past. If a project still uses 2025.1, have its owner confirm the migration status, build and deployment path before the next change.

For classic CRM cards, the spring release lists 31 October 2026. The current migration guide instead says cards are removed from customer views on 2 November, with migration tooling available until 1 December. The tooling window does not mean old cards remain visible through November.

I would plan to finish before 31 October and confirm the guidance with the app owner. The classic CRM card migration guide compares the sources and covers testing and view replacement. Sidebar placement alone does not identify a legacy card.

What I would prioritize
Check maintenance first. Confirm who owns custom apps, their supported version and any legacy-card replacement.
Choose one pilot. Test an agent or dataset against a defined task, with an owner, review criteria and usage limits.
Expand after review. Use the observed corrections, handovers and costs to decide what is worth keeping.

Questions about how these changes fit your setup? You're welcome to compare notes.
